newsitem.title: USA: GM shows resilience in Canadian auto strike.
newsitem.headline: GM shows resilience in Canadian auto strike.

text.p: General Motors Corp. continued to show resilience in keeping its U.S. factories running Thursday despite the complete shutdown of its Canadian operations.

The automaker said it was forced to idle only 100 more workers at its Ypsilanti, Mich., transmission plant on Thursday, bringing the total number of U.S. employees affected by the eight-day-old Canadian Auto Workers strike to 1,950.
About 625 workers in Mexico at GM's Delphi Packard Electric Division, who make wiring harnesses for Canadian-built vehicles, also were idled as of Thursday.
In March, one week after the United Auto Workers union struck GM's Dayton, Ohio, brake plants, about 16 GM assembly plants and 55,000 workers were idled.
Analysts said the more muted effects of the Canadian strike reflected better preparation by GM, which had ample warning of the walkout from Canadian Auto Workers President Buzz Hargrove.

GM Canada workers began an escalating walkout on Oct. 2, striking assembly plants in Oshawa, Ontario, and Ste. Therese, Quebec, first, leaving some critical parts plants to operate for several more days, which allowed GM to stockpile parts. The last of GM Canada's 26,000 workers hit the picket lines Wednesday night.

"This strike was hardly unexpected. The Canadian Auto Workers made a central point of saying they were prepared for a strike and prepared for a long one," said Harley Shaiken, a professor of labor relations at the University of California-Berkeley.

Still, he said GM's operations will inevitably grind to a halt, with assembly plants beginning to shut down next week. The 17-day Datyton strike ultimately forced GM to lay off 175,800 U.S. workers and halt production at 26 of its 29 assembly plants in the United States, Canada and Mexico.
It reduced GM's first quarter profit by $900 million.
Meanwhile, in Toronto on Tuesday, there was dissent among CAW leaders about whether to begin bargaining with Ford Motor Co. before the GM Canada strike is settled.

"It is the position of the Ford bargaining council that we not set a strike deadline until such time as they reach a tentative settlement at General Motors," said Bob Such, chairman of the Canadian Auto Worker union's master bargaining committee at Ford.
"We don't feel it would be appropriate for us to move into Ford when the GM workers are on strike."
But Hargrove said the move to Ford from the stalled GM talks was still a possibility and would be considered by the union leadership this weekend.

"In fairness to (Such), that's not for him to decide... we start with me and my advisors talking this through this weekend as to whether or not that makes sense," Hargrove said. "I know the Ford committee has been less than enthusiastic about it."
Hargrove acknowledged he would have to get the unanimous approval of the GM and Ford union committees to move the negotiations on to Ford.
"If we think it makes sense, I have to convince (the GM committee), make sure they are comfortable with this... and then I have to get the Ford committee on side," said Hargrove.
GM master bargaining chairman Dave Vyse shook his head when asked if Hargrove would get approval from the GM council.
"Buzz would have to come up with a lot of good reasons (to change our minds)," said Vyse.
Ford Canada spokesman Jim Hartford said the company was ready to talk whenever the union decides to move to it.
Talks between GM and the UAW continued in Detroit Thursday. A GM spokesman said the two sides are continuing to make progrss.
